question: Why shouldn’t that worry me?

answer_md:
Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose. He describes teams he inherited as “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” His response was to remove barriers, make intent explicit, and push decisions to the people closest to the work.

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center, he designed a flat organization with team-level autonomy, collective ownership, and minimal middle layers. But practitioners coming from command-and-control organizations sometimes reverted to familiar habits: decisions drifted upward, teams waited for direction, and bottlenecks formed. Matt repeatedly reinforced the model. Team leads focused on removing obstacles rather than controlling outcomes, with clear guidelines connecting team decisions to project objectives.

He brought product managers, designers, and engineers together in balanced teams with shared ownership and decision-making authority. They prioritized essential features, delivered thin-slice, production-ready solutions, and used user feedback and continuous retrospectives to adjust their work. He paired that autonomy with automation, continuous delivery, and quality-first engineering practices.

When hierarchy made people reluctant to share ideas, Matt established weekly brainstorming sessions where ideas were considered without judgment. He emphasized the shared mission over individual accolades and recognized contributions that advanced project goals. He also paired senior engineers with junior team members, organized weekly tech talks with peer-led demos, and embedded learning in live client projects.

His coaching focused on helping teams think clearly, not just execute tasks. He used transparency, direct feedback, and open communication, while creating space for people to take risks and challenge assumptions. At the Cloud Innovation Center, teams achieved **4x delivery acceleration** after embracing lean product and modern engineering practices. The change did not happen overnight.

question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:
🐾 Perfect, here's what I found.

At **Norfolk Southern**, Matt’s initial emphasis on a balanced team and test-driven development did not prevent a quality crisis. During the Cloud Innovation Center’s first major engagement in early **2020**, the team was modernizing the legacy Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A couple of months in, as the pandemic moved work online, the client reported rising defects even though dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The credibility hit landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, who were already accustomed to waterfall delivery.

An engineer had been solutioning from his own interpretation rather than the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. Coverage looked complete while defects went undetected. The backlog also contained vague stories without defined scenarios or a definition of done.

Matt took ownership of the failure rather than defending the metrics. He ran a complete bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and showed the gaps openly, including the problems in the backlog. He rebuilt it with SMART, testable stories and brought frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to sit side by side with the team and redo the code and test cases.

Rather than relying on process changes alone, he used Samman-style coaching: boot camps, coding katas, practice learning sessions, and pairing engineers with subject-matter experts through an “I do, we do, you do” progression. He also restructured agile ceremonies and delivered product management and SMART story training.

Defect rates dropped, and the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. Client and account leadership confidence was restored through the open audit and visible improvement. The story does not give a numerical defect reduction.

question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:
🐾 There’s a concrete failure in Matt’s delivery leadership.

In one financial services platform modernization engagement, Matt was the tech lead responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. He relied on inherited documentation and assumed the identity and access management (IAM) controls, environment boundaries, and downstream access configurations were correct.

He focused on delivery pressures instead of validating access patterns. He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, implement compensating controls such as data masking and email interception, or verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed from downstream environments.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT containing unmasked production customer data. Communications went to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and worked collectively with the team on root cause analysis, remediation, and corrective controls. But that did not prevent an individual consequence: the client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt describes it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.”

This was not an intentional, low-stakes experiment. Matt’s stated responsibility was to ensure a safe environment, and he had relied on assumptions rather than verification. Afterward, he made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership “day-one leadership responsibilities” in his delivery approach.

answer_md:
🐾 I know just the story.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a **Fortune 500 financial services client**. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams running test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. He relied on that documentation rather than confirming it was accurate. He focused on delivery pressures instead of validating access patterns, did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, and did not verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been masked or scrubbed. He also had not implemented compensating controls such as data masking or email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**. The root causes were insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They worked collectively to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. The client nevertheless demanded that the tester be removed from the project, a systemic failure with an individual consequence.

Matt describes the lesson as “assumptions are risks in disguise.” IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach, rather than configurations he assumed were already correct.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s a specific example from **Norfolk Southern**.

A few months into modernizing its Revenue and Shipment Planning platform in early **2020**, the client reported rising defects even though the team’s dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. Matt took ownership of the failure rather than defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and showed the gaps openly. An engineer had been building from his own interpretation instead of the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. The backlog was also part of the problem: vague stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done.

Instead of treating this as an individual engineer’s problem or adding another reporting process, Matt rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories. He brought frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work alongside the engineers and redo the code and tests properly. Coaching followed an “I do, we do, you do” progression, supported by coding katas, boot camps, and practice sessions.

He then changed the daily workflow so the practices would survive after the experts left. Pairs rotated daily, test cases came before the solution, and standups checked that sequence rather than relying on coverage dashboards. During remote work, pairs traded drivers frequently to reduce fatigue and keep both engineers involved.

Defect rates dropped, and the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. Pairing and test-first remained the team’s default after the experts went home, and the failure mode that caused the crisis did not recur.

🐾 Found it!

Matt grew **Accenture’s** Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers to **150+ practitioners** over **4 years**. The documented starting point was a **10-person pilot**, rather than **4 people**. The challenge was not just hiring: many new joiners lacked hands-on cloud-native or Agile experience, and the organization needed hiring, development, evaluation, and promotion processes without adding middle-management layers.

Matt built a hiring engine across **4 sourcing channels**: internal bench search, campus recruiting, contract-to-hire, and approved job requisitions. He participated in Georgia Tech recruiting, job fairs, and hackathons. Candidates completed hands-on auditions: TDD pairing for engineers, and live scoping or wireframing for product managers and designers. Matt held the closing interview and made every final hiring decision. During scaling pushes, the process handled **15 to 20 auditions per week**, producing **4 to 6 net-new practitioners per week**. Interviewers were capped at **2 interview slots per week** to protect delivery time.

New hires progressed through “I do, we do, you do” learning, tailored technical training, and round-robin pairing with experienced practitioners. Teams practiced pair programming, TDD, CI/CD, user research, and Build-Measure-Learn cycles. Skills matrices, mentoring, peer-led tech talks, and career development sessions continued after onboarding.

Matt kept the organization deliberately flat, with **11 to 13 practice and client leads** reporting directly to him. Experienced engineers served as team anchors rather than another management layer. Monday allocation reviews assigned practitioners across client engagements, training, and accelerator development. Because managers did not sit on daily teams, evaluations drew on evidence from recent pair partners, product managers, and anchors. Matt ran feedback capture, promotion calibration, compensation allocation, and remediation decisions.

The organization reached **150+ practitioners**, with near-zero attrition in the first **2 years**. Across the centers, **10-person balanced teams** delivered equivalent output to traditional **20-person teams**, with **4X faster velocity** and zero-defect deployments. Delivery excellence and client advocacy contributed to **\$100M+ in repeatable business** by **FY23**.

Matt’s payments work includes payment-engine delivery and legacy-system consolidation at **JP Morgan Chase**, Virtual Payments Platform integration at **American Express**, and cross-border workflow design at **RBC**.

question: Sure.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s what Matt worked on at **Norfolk Southern**.

As a Director at **Accenture**, Matt led modernization of **Norfolk Southern’s** Revenue and Shipment Planning platform, the Cloud Innovation Center’s first engagement. Its mainframe dated to the **1970s**. Orders could fall out unnoticed until customers called, business rules lived in COBOL and assembly maintained by a shrinking workforce, and clerks manually handled waybill and rating fallout. The work also faced resistance across the client’s mainframe-oriented organization, account leadership accustomed to waterfall, and a delivery team learning new practices during the pandemic.

Matt brought cross-workstream representatives into domain-driven design and event storming sessions to map business functions, data flows, and dependencies. He used the Boris Exercise and SNAP-E documentation to define APIs, boundaries, and integration requirements. Rather than replace everything at once, the mainframe stayed the system of record while APIs, microservices, and CockroachDB rose beside it. Change data capture synchronized the platforms, and reconciliation checked that nothing was lost. When the client grew restless for tangible progress, Matt brought revenue management into the innovation hub to co-create the Shipper Revenue System workspace through personas, prototypes, and weekly build-measure-learn iterations.

He also addressed a quality crisis directly. Despite near-complete test coverage, defects were rising. Matt took ownership in front of the client and account leadership, audited the code and tests, and found tests written after code and backlog stories without defined scenarios. He rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought frontend and backend TDD experts alongside the team for hands-on coaching.

For enablement, Matt led a **2-day** CIC Academy course twice monthly over **6 months**. He worked through resistance to pairing by letting the client experience it, then rotated scarce domain knowledge through “I do, we do, you do” practice. Client contributors learned Angular, Node, Spring Boot, and cloud-native concepts.

The MVP launched covering **95%** of targeted use cases. EDI validation caught fallout proactively, the client co-created in weekly iterations, and client contributors gained the skills to support and manage the new application after **Accenture** rolled off.

Matt used measurable delivery results, budget and cost management, and a “cost-to-fix vs. benefit comparison” to make investment cases. His stories do not specify an exact ROI formula or a calculated ROI percentage.

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Centers, clients wanted to move away from waterfall delivery, feature factories, and siloed teams. Pair programming raised concerns about cost. Engineers working in isolation were also dealing with bugs, frequent rework, missed deadlines, and difficult onboarding for junior developers.

Matt addressed the investment question by demonstrating velocity gains and quality improvements that offset the investment. He owned full P&L accountability for the Atlanta and Tampa centers, including budget and cost management. He tracked chargeability, unbillable downtime, and contractor spend, requiring internal bench deployment before approving external contractors.

At **RBC**, Matt worked with the enterprise architecture team on a transparent “cost-to-fix vs. benefit comparison.” Code reviews, interviews, and architectural heat maps identified that WebSeries lacked the modularity the bank required. The assessment prevented investment in that platform path and enabled technical resources to move to higher-priority initiatives. No dollar savings were recorded in that story.

At **Fiserv**, the financial results were recorded separately: recovery of an **\$8.5M** program delivered **3%** under budget, preserving **\$255K** in margin, avoiding **\$500K** in contractual penalties, and securing a **\$3M** extension.
